candidate.title: Eric Sampson vs Lance Bush: Is Moral Realism True? (2022)
candidate.label: Moral realism and stance-independent reasons
candidate.summary: Sampson narrowly prevails by defining a limited realism and defending its intelligibility, while Bush supplies powerful underdetermination and genealogy challenges that remain evidentially incomplete.
candidate.sourceNote: This assessment uses a complete timestamp-preserving Whisper transcription reconstructed from twelve overlapping audio chunks; all selected speaker attributions were high confidence, and quotations were checked against the locked source events.
candidate.scoringNote: These AI-generated scores were computed once from a frozen 25-move ledger after two isolated primary judgments and anonymous adjudication of all 10 extracted disagreements. No attribution uncertainty triggered an audio check. The displayed 82–81 result is immutable; publication prose and the later rhetorical-tag review could not change it.

con.name: Moral realism is unintelligible or unjustified
con.speaker: Lance Bush

pro.text: I should save this kid even if I didn't want to
pro.context: Sampson uses the rescue judgment as prima facie personal evidence that at least one normative requirement applies independently of an agent's desires.

con.text: inadvertently projecting culturally acquired values onto the world
con.context: Bush proposes psychological projection as a simpler rival explanation for realist belief, shifting the dispute from bare intelligibility toward comparative explanatory adequacy.

sections.title: Positions, semantics, and the scope of realism

pro.words: Sampson defines realism as cognitivism, non-nihilism, and the stance-independent truth of at least some moral beliefs, thereby fixing a deliberately limited affirmative target.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The three-part definition cleanly separates truth-evaluable moral belief, the existence of some moral truths, and independence from individual or cultural reactions, establishing an unusually precise motion-level target. Principal limitation: Definition supplies conceptual organization rather than evidence, and Sampson does not show that his taxonomy exhausts relevant realism or that actual moral discourse instantiates every identified component. Live burden: He must progress from the coherent possibility of stance-independent truth to warranted belief in such truth, while preserving his careful existential scope against Bush's semantic and genealogical challenges. Locked score: The move excels in logical coherence, responsiveness, precision, and calibration, but its evidential contribution remains properly modest because fixing the proposition cannot establish that proposition's truth.

con.words: Bush rejects any uniform semantics for ordinary moral claims, instead proposing an unfinished mixture of relativist, error-theoretic, and noncognitive interpretations across different speakers.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush carefully resists forcing every moral utterance into one anti-realist model, and his pluralism fairly recognizes that speakers may express propositions, attitudes, or locally relativized commitments differently. Principal limitation: The excerpt contrasts possible semantic theories without presenting representative linguistic evidence, and its promised positive combination remains insufficiently specified to explain which uses receive which analysis. Live burden: Bush must demonstrate actual variation, formulate principled classification criteria, and explain why pluralism threatens Sampson's existential thesis that merely some communities make shared truth-evaluable claims. Locked score: The move is coherent, responsive, and admirably calibrated, yet limited evidential warrant and incomplete positive detail prevent semantic diversity from establishing either global indeterminacy or the motion-level rejection of realism.

pro.words: Sampson answers pluralism by arguing that realism needs only some communities whose shared moral assertions express beliefs capable of truth or falsity assessment.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson exploits the existential scope of his definition precisely, conceding broad semantic variation while preserving cognitivism wherever communities share moral propositions that they can dispute as true or false. Principal limitation: Plausible communal coordination does not independently prove that the relevant utterances express beliefs, and truth evaluability establishes neither actual truth nor the stance independence required by realism. Live burden: He must support the semantic characterization and then defend non-nihilism and independence, rather than allowing successful resistance to a universal objection to masquerade as positive ontological evidence. Locked score: This is a highly responsive, logically economical, clear, and charitable local rebuttal whose disciplined quantifiers protect one necessary realist component without completing the affirmative's larger evidential burden.

con.words: Bush concedes that semantic uncertainty does not refute local realism but argues it removes realism's claimed common-sense presumption and associated burden-shifting advantage.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush recalibrates rather than overclaims, correctly observing that uncertainty about ordinary semantic commitments can undercut an appeal to common sense even when local cognitivism remains entirely possible. Principal limitation: He supplies no documented findings concerning ordinary usage or its prevalence, so the removal of default status depends on an empirical premise presented only conditionally and impressionistically. Live burden: Bush must establish what nonphilosophers mean, show why those patterns govern metaphysical presumption, and clarify what affirmative burden changes after Sampson has already narrowed realism existentially. Locked score: The move displays strong coherence, responsiveness, clarity, and exceptional charity, but its indirect relevance and unsupported empirical foundation make it a useful dialectical qualification rather than substantive evidence against realism.

pro.words: Sampson argues that a drowning child's welfare, threatened suffering, and the minimal cost of rescue are intelligible reasons to act regardless of the rescuer's goals.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The rescue case answers Bush with concrete situational facts, identifying the endangered child's welfare, familial suffering, comparative benefit, and minimal cost as recognizable considerations favoring immediate intervention. Principal limitation: Saying that the child matters embeds the contested normative premise, so the example illuminates how external reasons appear without independently proving that their authority is stance independent. Live burden: Sampson must distinguish eliciting a powerful shared intuition from explaining its truth conditions and show why relational, constructivist, or psychological accounts cannot accommodate the same verdict. Locked score: The move is exceptionally relevant, clear, and responsive and gives substantial intuitive warrant for intelligibility, although its logical bridge from apparent importance to objective reason remains contestable.

con.words: Bush contends that reasons become intelligible only relative to desires or standards, using hunger to illustrate why desire-independent reasons purportedly make no sense.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The food example gives Bush's relational alternative concrete structure, clearly contrasting reasons generated by an agent's wants with Sampson's proposed reasons that apply regardless of those wants. Principal limitation: One intelligible desire-relative reason does not establish that every intelligible reason must be relational, while Bush's personal incomprehension cannot itself demonstrate contradiction, emptiness, or universal unintelligibility. Live burden: He must define the governing standard of intelligibility, exclude primitive favoring relations without presupposing relationalism, and engage the strongest external-reason account rather than merely reporting unfamiliarity. Locked score: The move directly contacts a central affirmative burden and is relevant if proven, but weak universal warrant, incomplete conceptual analysis, and limited charity substantially constrain its force.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: Bush uses his personal comprehension of relational reasons and incomprehension of external reasons to support a universal distinction.

pro.words: Sampson insists that the child's importance and rescue benefit constitute the requested explanation, treating Bush's continued incomprehension as failure to grasp a primitive reason.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson refuses an infinite regress of explanations and identifies a definite stopping point, treating the child's welfare and inexpensive rescue as publicly stated facts that normatively explain intervention. Principal limitation: Repeating that the child matters may clarify the proposed reason without vindicating its irreducible authority, and the move too quickly converts Bush's dissatisfaction into defective understanding. Live burden: Sampson must justify primitive normative explanation, distinguish it from mere assertion, and offer some basis for preferring his stopping point over Bush's desire-relative reconstruction of the same conduct. Locked score: The response is direct, coherent, and unusually clear about its explanatory commitment, yet intuitive warrant and limited engagement with the rival analysis leave stance-independent truth unestablished.

con.words: Bush argues that privately claiming to understand stance-independent reasons is inadequate unless one can publicly explain what those reasons mean and how they make sense.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush identifies an important dialectical difference between experiencing comprehension and communicating an explanation capable of showing another participant what a disputed concept means and how it operates. Principal limitation: He leaves the required explanatory standard unspecified and risks assuming that genuine understanding always permits reductive elaboration, thereby excluding primitive concepts through a criterion the argument never defends. Live burden: Bush must explain what public account would suffice, demonstrate that stance-independent favoring fails that standard, and establish that comparable foundational concepts do not face the same stopping point. Locked score: The reply sharply advances the intelligibility dispute and directly tests Sampson's example, but limited evidence and an underdefined criterion prevent reported explanatory dissatisfaction from proving conceptual incoherence.

sections.title: Corroboration, intuition, and prima facie justification

pro.words: Sampson replies that non-natural moral facts predictably lack empirical detectors, so failure to supply engineering-style tests provides little evidence against his ontology.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson correctly notes that evidence must fit the proposed ontology, making absence of a physical moral-property detector expected under non-naturalism rather than a surprising failure that straightforwardly disconfirms it. Principal limitation: Classifying moral facts as non-natural blocks one evidential demand but supplies no alternative access method, and may insulate realism unless independent warrant constrains that classification. Live burden: He must explain how competing normative claims can be assessed, identify reliability conditions for intuition, and show that ontological mismatch does not become immunity from meaningful epistemic scrutiny. Locked score: The response is logically coherent, precise, calibrated, and directly responsive, yet it protects realism from an unsuitable test without positively meeting Bush's broader corroboration challenge.

con.words: Bush contrasts morality with engineering, biology, and medicine, arguing that realism lacks comparable independent consequences capable of corroborating theories and adjudicating disagreements.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The cross-disciplinary comparison crystallizes a serious epistemic asymmetry, asking what publicly accessible consequence could discriminate rival moral accounts when first-order intuitions and judgments remain fundamentally contested. Principal limitation: Empirical disciplines may set an inappropriate standard for non-natural facts, and Bush does not establish that every justified domain requires detection, prediction, or practical confirmation of the illustrated kind. Live burden: He must specify a suitably general corroboration requirement, defend its applicability to normativity, and explain whether coherent reflection or explanatory success could satisfy it without becoming circular. Locked score: The move strongly advances the public-adjudication burden through clear and relevant comparisons, but incomplete defense of their comparability prevents absent empirical testing from independently defeating realism.

pro.words: Sampson argues that his clear intuition of an obligation to rescue despite contrary desire prima facie justifies personal belief in stance-independent normative truth.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson explicitly connects a vivid seeming of obligation, its asserted independence from desire, and a limited conclusion about his own prima facie justification rather than claiming universal demonstration. Principal limitation: The inference compresses the crucial transition from an experience with objective phenomenology to warranted realism, without comparing error, projection, relational, or constructivist explanations of that experience. Live burden: He must defend intuition's reliability, address genealogical defeaters, and explain why the content seeming stance independent supplies evidence for corresponding facts rather than merely culturally structured cognition. Locked score: This central affirmative route is clear, calibrated, responsive, and personally evidential, but its limited corroboration and underdeveloped reliability warrant prevent the paradigm case from settling the public dispute.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: Sampson treats his clear personal seeming of a desire-independent rescue obligation as justification for realism.

con.words: Bush argues that agreement about rescuing the child cannot corroborate realism because anti-realists may endorse precisely the same action while rejecting stance-independent truths.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush cleanly separates first-order normative agreement from second-order metaethical commitment, and his own endorsement of rescue provides a concrete compatibility case showing that identical verdicts can receive rival explanations. Principal limitation: Demonstrating underdetermination by one judgment does not show that every pattern of deliberation, error, or convergence is equally compatible with all theories, nor directly answer Sampson's ontology-mismatch reply. Live burden: Bush must extend the compatibility argument across the realist's total evidence and compare how well competing accounts explain obligation's apparent authority rather than merely reproducing behavioral conclusions. Locked score: The move is exceptionally precise, charitable, coherent, and dialectically relevant, successfully blocking simple agreement as unique confirmation while leaving broader comparative explanation open.

sections.title: Deep disagreement and the Zorpian comparison

pro.words: Sampson accepts that intuitions may fail to persuade others while maintaining that they remain genuine prima facie evidence for the individuals experiencing them.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson preserves the exact scope of his claim by distinguishing personal justification from interpersonal persuasion, incorporating Bush's strongest concession rather than pretending that private evidence automatically resolves public disagreement. Principal limitation: He asserts intuition's evidential status without developing reliability, independence, or resistance to genealogical defeat, so the distinction protects a modest entitlement rather than realism generally. Live burden: Sampson must show that his seeming is undefeated, explain why its origin plausibly tracks normative truth, and supply resources for choosing between equally sincere incompatible intuitions. Locked score: The reply demonstrates excellent logical coherence, responsiveness, precision, and calibration and successfully defends prima facie personal justification, while openly leaving public corroboration and comparative metaethical confirmation unresolved.

con.words: Bush grants that realist intuition may personally justify Sampson while denying that such private evidence can substantially resolve a shared metaethical dispute.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush accepts Sampson's carefully limited justificatory claim and sharply distinguishes evidence rationally available to its possessor from evidence capable of adjudicating disagreement among participants lacking the same seeming. Principal limitation: The Bigfoot comparison vividly illustrates privacy but may obscure important differences between isolated perceptual experience and pervasive reflective judgment, while private evidence need not be epistemically negligible. Live burden: Bush must identify why moral intuition is unreliable or comparatively weak, not merely unshared, and explain what public evidence could address metaethical questions without presupposing his preferred standards. Locked score: The reply is highly responsive, precise, charitable, and powerful against dialectical overreach, although it challenges interpersonal force more successfully than Sampson's conceded personal justification.

pro.words: Sampson replies that genuinely attitude-independent Zorpian reasons would simply be moral or normative facts under another name, not a separate parody domain.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson catches a terminological consequence of Bush's stipulation, since universally applicable reasons satisfying the realist structure belong within the normative domain regardless of an alien label. Principal limitation: Identifying the domain does not resolve the thought experiment's central epistemic problem, namely how equally confident communities could reach incompatible substantive verdicts through apparently parallel methods. Live burden: Sampson must break the reliability symmetry, explain why human rescue intuitions track genuine reasons while Zorpian competitive intuitions do not, and avoid assuming the disputed normative properties. Locked score: The response is clear and locally coherent but only partially responsive, offering useful conceptual housekeeping while leaving the analogy's strongest evidential challenge substantially untouched and insufficiently warranted.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: Sampson responds to Zorpian parity by classifying attitude-independent alien reasons as moral facts under another name.

con.words: Bush imagines competitively evolved Zorpians with contrary but structurally similar normative intuitions, challenging whether Sampson's method can distinguish truth from cultural conditioning.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The detailed alien society converts abstract reliability worries into a discriminating parity test, showing how contrary attitudes, intuitions, and realist arguments might arise from an alternative selective history. Principal limitation: The analogy depends on matching every epistemically relevant feature, and its deliberately abhorrent competitive norms may encourage intuitive rejection without establishing that Zorpian evidence genuinely equals human evidence. Live burden: Bush must specify the parity conditions, explain why evolutionary origin defeats rather than merely causes belief, and show that no independent substantive reason breaks the symmetry. Locked score: The thought experiment strongly pressures intuitive realism with considerable relevance, clarity, and methodological ingenuity, but its reliability conclusion remains conditional upon an incompletely defended comparison.

sections.title: Primitive concepts, circular definitions, and practical force

pro.words: Sampson treats cross-position philosophical understanding of normative discourse as defeasible evidence, shifting onto Bush the burden of explaining a purportedly widespread illusion.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson uses disciplinary uptake modestly as burden-shifting evidence rather than conclusive truth, noting that even many anti-realists competently discuss the concepts Bush characterizes as unintelligible or gibberish. Principal limitation: The asserted consensus lacks documentation, overstates its prevalence, and may reflect shared training or professional selection rather than reliable recognition of coherent stance-independent properties. Live burden: Sampson must substantiate the pattern and explain why sustained inferential practice indicates intelligibility, while Bush owes a developed alternative account if he maintains a universal nonsense diagnosis. Locked score: The reply is responsive, comparatively charitable, and explanatorily significant, but its evidential force remains defeasible because testimony and professional competence support conceptual usability more directly than realism's truth.

con.words: Bush argues that widespread professions of understanding cannot establish intelligibility, comparing them with consensus about contradictory or invented concepts that remain meaningless.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush correctly denies entailment from widespread claimed comprehension to genuine intelligibility, and his counterexamples reveal that testimony alone cannot guarantee that a purported concept possesses coherent content. Principal limitation: Comparing stance-independent reasons with square circles or deliberate nonsense assumes the relevant defect without demonstrating contradiction, inferential emptiness, or comparable semantic failure in normative discourse. Live burden: Bush must provide a positive criterion of meaningfulness and show how realist reasons violate it, rather than relying on skeptical possibilities that could undermine many theoretically primitive concepts. Locked score: The move directly limits consensus-based proof with clear reasoning, but weak analogy, underspecified standards, and incomplete charity leave the original intelligibility objection protected rather than affirmatively established.

pro.words: Sampson argues categorical norms perform indispensable work by assessing and recommending changes to goals, rather than merely directing means toward antecedently accepted ends.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson identifies a precise functional gap in hypothetical imperatives, since conditionals can organize means under existing goals while categorical norms purport to evaluate which goals agents should adopt. Principal limitation: Describing this useful role does not establish that corresponding stance-independent facts exist, and the claimed authority to revise ends remains the very normative feature under dispute. Live burden: He must show that deliberative goal criticism cannot be reconstructed through coherence, information, higher-order desires, or social standards, then connect irreducible function to ontological truth. Locked score: The reply is conceptually clear, directly responsive, and relevant to normative explanation, yet its central existential inference remains assumed, making functional indispensability suggestive rather than demonstrative.

con.words: Bush analyzes apparent logical prescriptions as hypothetical imperatives relative to an agent's goals, denying that logic provides an analogue for categorical moral normativity.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush supplies a substantive conditional analysis rather than merely rejecting Sampson's analogy, explaining how logical standards may guide agents who antecedently seek truth, consistency, or successful inference. Principal limitation: He does not establish that every epistemic demand is hypothetical, especially when logic appears capable of criticizing irrational aims or inconsistent reasoning independently of an agent's endorsement. Live burden: Bush must defend exhaustive conditionalism, separate practical from epistemic normativity, and explain whether agents have reasons to revise truth-indifferent goals without importing categorical standards elsewhere. Locked score: The move is coherent, clear, and responsive to the neighboring-domain analogy, but limited warrant and untreated categorical roles prevent logic's conditional reconstruction from establishing that moral reasons are relational.

sections.title: Explanatory parsimony and the genealogy of moral belief

pro.words: Sampson concedes that confirmed selection effects could trouble realism but emphasizes that Bush's current proposal remains an untested blueprint awaiting empirical evidence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson precisely tracks the hypothesis's status, granting its potential significance while correctly observing that a proposed mechanism cannot discharge an empirical explanatory burden before its predictions receive evidential support. Principal limitation: Blocking an unconfirmed defeater does not itself provide positive evidence for stance-independent truth, and disciplinary intelligibility could remain evidentially weak even if Bush's particular hypothesis fails. Live burden: Sampson should clarify the affirmative value of professional understanding, while Bush must supply the promised comparison and mechanism before invoking selection as an actual undercutting explanation. Locked score: This exceptionally responsive, coherent, clear, and charitable reply fairly conditions future consequences on investigation, decisively preserving the local defense without exaggerating what evidential suspension establishes for realism.

con.words: Bush proposes that philosophers self-selecting into a narrow discipline may explain their unusual reports of normative intelligibility better than reliable conceptual recognition does.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush accepts the explanatory burden and offers an empirically testable population contrast, predicting that laypeople will report substantially less understanding or endorsement than academic philosophers selected into the discourse. Principal limitation: The prediction remains prospective, with no survey, sampling design, operational definition, or causal mechanism showing that selection rather than expertise produces the purported disciplinary difference. Live burden: Bush must gather comparative evidence, separate intelligibility from truth endorsement, control relevant education effects, and show why any observed disparity undermines rather than merely localizes conceptual competence. Locked score: The hypothesis is coherent, responsive, clear, and cautiously stated, but weak present warrant makes it a promising research blueprint rather than a completed explanation or defeater.

pro.words: Sampson objects that psychological parsimony is irrelevant unless both theories explain identical phenomena, whereas anti-realism excludes the normative facts realism seeks to explain.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson targets the crucial equal-explananda condition for legitimate simplicity comparisons, noting that an apparently lean theory wins nothing by deleting phenomena its rival regards as requiring explanation. Principal limitation: Counting genuine normative facts among the data assumes the realism at issue, while Bush primarily offers to explain moral beliefs and behavior rather than antecedently conceded normative entities. Live burden: Sampson must identify independent evidence for irreducible normative explananda or observable losses in Bush's account, and Bush must explain obligation's apparent authority rather than only its psychological production. Locked score: The reply is precise, highly responsive, and logically important as a conditional objection, but limited independent warrant prevents it from overturning parsimony rather than postponing comparison.

tags.label: Begging the question
tags.context: Sampson says anti-realism is not parsimonious because its psychological account omits genuine normative facts from its explananda.

con.words: Bush offers psychological projection of culturally acquired values as a parsimonious explanation of realist belief and behavior that avoids positing stance-independent normative facts.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush advances beyond personal incomprehension by proposing a positive abductive competitor, explaining realist conviction through cultural acquisition, psychological projection, and inadvertent reification of internal values as external features. Principal limitation: The mechanisms are plausible but unsupported comparatively, and explaining why people believe a proposition does not establish its falsity or show that a truth-tracking explanation adds no value. Live burden: Bush must identify the complete explananda, provide evidence for projection, specify his simplicity metric, and demonstrate superior fit over models in which cultural processes sometimes track normative truth. Locked score: The move is relevant, coherent, clear, and constructively responsive, but insufficient evidence and premature best-explanation language leave the parsimonious genealogy materially underdeveloped.

con.words: Bush closes by explaining moral cognition as culturally and biologically contingent human dispositions, rather than detection of universal or fundamental stance-independent facts.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Bush supplies a broad naturalistic genealogy capable of unifying moral variation, emotional force, behavioral regularity, and inherited dispositions without initially positing a separate realm of normative properties. Principal limitation: Cultural and biological causation remains compatible with truth, and the move presents no concrete historical, comparative, or biological evidence connecting contingency to systematic unreliability. Live burden: Bush must show why the identified processes track fitness or coordination instead of normative truth, predict characteristic errors, and outperform coexistence models where genealogy and realism jointly explain belief. Locked score: This relevant, clear, calibrated motion-level constructive improves the positive anti-realist case, but the uncompleted inference from causal origin to epistemic defeat prevents genealogy from conclusively rejecting realism.

strengths: Sampson defines a deliberately existential realism, then repeatedly preserves that limited scope against semantic pluralism instead of defending unnecessary uniformity across all moral discourse.

His rescue example and replies about welfare make stance-independent reasons concretely intelligible, while his distinction between personal justification and persuasion accurately absorbs Bush's strongest concession.
He manages burdens exceptionally well against speculative selection effects, granting that future confirmation could hurt realism while refusing to treat an empirical blueprint as present evidence.

blunders.text: Sampson repeatedly moves too quickly from objective-seeming intuitions to objective facts, without supplying a reliability account capable of defeating projection or incompatible Zorpian intuitions.
His answer to Zorpian parity largely relabels attitude-independent alien reasons as moral facts, leaving the actual problem of discriminating contradictory substantive judgments unresolved.
His parsimony reply risks assuming realism by counting normative facts among established explananda, rather than independently identifying phenomena that psychological anti-realism cannot explain.

strengths: Bush consistently distinguishes first-order agreement from metaethical confirmation, showing that anti-realists can endorse rescue while denying that the shared verdict uniquely supports realism.

His private-evidence objection is carefully calibrated, conceding personal justification while explaining why unshared intuition cannot independently adjudicate a public dispute between rival metaethical theories.

The Zorpian case and psychological genealogy jointly create a serious reliability challenge by showing how culturally contingent processes might generate confident realist-seeming judgments with incompatible contents.

blunders.text: Bush's foundational relationalism leans heavily on personal unintelligibility and a desire-relative example, neither of which establishes the universal claim that all intelligible reasons are conditional.

His comparison with empirical disciplines demands independent corroboration without adequately defending why non-natural normative claims must satisfy engineering-style prediction or detection standards.

His academic selection and cultural-biological explanations remain largely prospective, lacking data, operational criteria, or a demonstrated link from causal contingency to epistemic unreliability or falsity.

logicalExtension.label: AI-generated extension; not transcript content or wording attributable to either speaker.

finalArgument.thesis: The best cumulative case for non-naturalist realism treats normative authority as a stable explanatory constraint on deliberation, not merely as an introspective feeling or semantic convention.
premises: Competent deliberators distinguish facts about their current goals from judgments that those goals themselves merit criticism, revision, or abandonment despite motivational resistance.
Purely instrumental conditionals can recommend effective means under accepted ends, but cannot generate criticism of every antecedent end without appealing to some further evaluative standard.

Paradigm judgments such as inexpensive rescue remain stable under fuller information, impartial role reversal, and correction of factual error, providing defeasible evidence beyond immediate preference.
Genealogical explanations of how normative beliefs arise undermine them only when connected to unreliability, and cultural causation alone is compatible with imperfect recognition of genuine reasons.
A theory recognizing stance-independent reasons explains goal criticism, normative error, and deliberative improvement more completely than a theory describing only attitudes and causal dispositions.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, absent a demonstrated reliability defeater or equally complete relational reconstruction, some stance-independent normative truths remain the best explanation of disciplined deliberative practice.

newArguments.title: Counterfactual deliberative invariance
newArguments.text: Test normative judgments across controlled changes in personal desire, social approval, and strategic advantage while preserving all nonnormative facts. If judgments about rescue, cruelty, or arbitrary harm remain stable after agents vividly reverse roles and eliminate self-interest, that invariance is unexpected on a simple preference-projection model. It supplies new, defeasible evidence that deliberation tracks considerations represented as authoritative independently of the evaluator's present stance.

newArguments.title: Normative error asymmetry
newArguments.text: Realist discourse distinguishes changing one's mind because preferences changed from discovering that earlier preferences were unjustified. A purely descriptive genealogy can explain both psychological transitions, but it threatens to erase the practiced asymmetry between mere conversion and correction. Realism gains explanatory support if anti-realism cannot reconstruct that asymmetry without introducing standards that evaluate attitudes independently of whichever attitudes an agent presently holds.

newArguments.title: Higher-order regress constraint
newArguments.text: Relational accounts can explain criticism of a goal by invoking a higher-order goal, but any challenged higher-order commitment then requires another endorsed standard. Either the chain terminates in an arbitrary attitude, undermining rational criticism of foundational ends, or it terminates in a consideration with authority not borrowed from desire. The latter stopping point functions as a stance-independent reason and independently reinforces Sampson's primitive normative explanation.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest anti-realist conclusion is epistemic rather than dogmatically eliminative: available moral experience does not warrant adding stance-independent facts to relational and psychological explanations.
premises: The same first-order judgments and behaviors are compatible with realism, constructivism, expressivism, and sophisticated relational accounts, so agreement alone cannot discriminate their truth conditions.

Intuitions that present requirements as objective are generated through culturally and biologically shaped cognitive systems whose reliability concerning non-natural properties has not been independently established.

Realism offers no public procedure that reliably distinguishes accurate normative intuition from equally confident incompatible intuition while avoiding reliance upon further contested normative judgments.

Relational standards, instrumental reasoning, social coordination, and psychological projection jointly explain moral language, motivation, disagreement, and behavioral stability without presupposing stance-independent properties.
When rival theories explain the accessible evidence comparably, rational ontology favors the account with fewer unsupported entities until distinctive evidence for the costlier account appears.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, present evidence warrants withholding belief in stance-independent moral facts, even if it does not demonstrate that every possible realist proposition is false or meaningless.

newArguments.title: Calibration without access
newArguments.text: Reliable faculties ordinarily permit some calibration through feedback, convergence under improved conditions, or identifiable correction procedures. Realist intuition lacks an uncontested external target, and every proposed correction appears to use additional intuitions from the same disputed source. This does not prove universal error, but it lowers confidence comparatively because a method that cannot distinguish success from internally coherent failure provides weak grounds for positing an inaccessible normative domain.

newArguments.title: Explanatory intervention test
newArguments.text: Consider interventions that alter upbringing, group incentives, emotional conditioning, or perceived social roles while leaving nonnormative circumstances fixed. If moral confidence and apparent self-evidence vary predictably with those interventions, psychological models gain risky, testable predictions that bare realism does not generate. Realism could coexist with those effects, but coexistence adds no explanatory advantage unless it separately predicts which resulting judgments are accurate and why.

newArguments.title: Reference indeterminacy challenge
newArguments.text: Even granting that moral sentences express truth-evaluable beliefs, realism must explain how speakers causally isolated from non-natural properties successfully refer to the same properties rather than merely coordinating on shared attitudes and inferential roles. Divergent communities may exhibit equally coherent usage while purportedly targeting incompatible normative structures. Without a reference-fixing account, local cognitivism secures propositional form but not determinate contact with stance-independent truth.
